turns.doctor_question: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you into the clinic today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, thank you. I... I honestly don't even know if a doctor can do anything about this, but I came because, well, it’s my husband’s sister. My sister-in-law. She has been working this whole family business situation for a while now, and it’s just got me wound up so tight. 

See, she’s been maneuvering things behind the scenes so she can get total control of the money. Our money. And she’s actively trying to push me out of all the decisions. I mean, I see her doing it. She’ll come over, start asking about the accounts, acting like she is just trying to help out since I am at home and not working right now, but I know exactly what she's up to. 

And the frustrating part, the really frustrating part that just makes my blood boil, is that my husband and everyone else, they just try to smooth it over. They say she is just being helpful, or she is just looking out for the family's future. But they don't see the way she looks at me when they leave the room. They don't hear the little comments she makes under her breath. No matter how folks try to smooth it all over and tell me I am just imagining things, I know what I’ve been seeing for more than a year now. A little over a year, actually, ever since last fall. It’s like this slow, calculated takeover, and nobody believes me when I try to explain the puzzle pieces I've put together, but I'm not blind, you know? I see exactly what she's doing and I just don't know how much more of it I can take.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes a fixed, persistent belief that her sister-in-law is plotting to take control of the family money, which she maintains despite others telling her she is imagining things.
symptom_reasoning.S058: The patient explicitly states that the situation has her feeling 'wound up so tight,' indicating physical tension or feeling keyed up.

top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever heard voices, whispering, or other sounds when no one was around or that other people couldn't hear?
turns.patient_response:
Voices? Like... like I'm crazy? No, no, no. I know why you're asking that, because I know that's what people think when a woman my age starts complaining about things nobody else wants to admit are happening. But I am not hearing things that aren't there. I don't hear ghosts or people whispering from the walls or the television talking to me or anything like that. 

The only whispering I hear—and I mean the only whispering—is when she is standing right there in my own house, thinking I'm out of earshot. It's real whispering. Like just last week, she was over, supposedly dropping off some bank statements for my husband, and I stepped into the laundry room to switch over a load of towels. I heard her whispering on her cell phone. Real whispering, from a real person, not in my head. And of course, the second I walked back into the kitchen, she snapped the phone shut and put on that fake little smile of hers. 

So no, when I'm alone in the house, it is perfectly quiet. Sometimes it's too quiet, honestly, since I'm not working right now and I'm just sitting there all day trying to piece together her next move. But I absolutely do not hear imaginary sounds, doctor. I just hear what she is actually saying when she thinks I'm too uneducated to notice.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed belief that another woman is plotting or acting against her, noting that others refuse to admit it is happening, which indicates delusional thinking.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies hearing voices, imaginary sounds, or whispering when no one is around.

turns.doctor_question: Outside of your sister-in-law, have you generally found that other people in your life, like friends, neighbors, or former coworkers, tend to take advantage of you or work against you?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, it's really just her. I mean, sure, you have your run-of-the-mill disagreements with people, like that one neighbor I had a few years back who would always let her dog do its business right on the edge of my lawn, and we had words about that, but that was just normal neighborhood stuff. It wasn't some big plot against me. And my old coworkers, back when I was still working, they were fine. I mean, we weren't best friends or anything, but we got along alright. We'd have coffee in the breakroom and complain about the boss, just like anybody else. 

It's just her. It's just my sister-in-law. That's what makes it so baffling to my husband, I think. He sees me getting along with the cashier at the grocery store, or chatting with the mailman, and then he sees how tense I get around his sister, and he just assumes I'm the one being difficult. But he doesn't understand that I don't go looking for trouble. I don't sit around thinking the whole world is out to get me. I really don't. It's just this one specific situation, with this one specific person who has decided she wants what is rightfully ours. 

If it were everybody, I'd probably think there was something wrong with me, you know? But it's not. I can go to church and talk to the ladies in the auxiliary, and everything is perfectly fine. Nobody there is trying to push me out of my own life. It's just her, and the way she has her claws dug into the family business, and the way she treats me like I'm some sort of obstacle she has to step over. So, no, I don't have problems with people generally. Just the one who is actually causing problems.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient reiterates her fixed, persecutory belief that her sister-in-law is plotting against her and trying to take what is rightfully hers, even while denying that she feels this way about people in general.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever felt like thoughts were being put into your head from the outside, or that your mind was being controlled by an external force?
turns.patient_response:
Put into my head? Like... like mind control? Oh, heavens, no. No, no, no. I mean, I know my thoughts are entirely my own. I sit there at the kitchen table with my coffee in the mornings, and I think about everything that's going on, sure. I turn it all over and over in my mind, trying to figure out how she managed to get my husband to agree to her looking over the new accounts, but those are absolutely my thoughts. Nobody is beaming them into my brain like some late-night science fiction movie, doctor. I might not have finished high school back in the day, but I have a perfectly sound mind, I promise you that. I am the one putting all these puzzle pieces together. It's just me in there. 

If anything, I honestly wish I could turn my brain off sometimes, because it just gets so incredibly exhausting constantly having to be the vigilant one. The one watching the bank statements, the one noticing the little smirks she gives when she thinks I'm looking the other way. But it's all me doing the noticing and the thinking. Nobody is controlling me from the outside. 

I think that's exactly why it upsets me so much when my husband acts like I'm losing my grip or just being hysterical. Because I am completely in control of my own faculties, and I know exactly what I'm seeing. Think about it—if some outside force really was controlling my mind, I'd probably be perfectly happy just sitting back and letting her steal us blind, wouldn't I? She'd probably prefer it if my mind was being controlled! But it's not. I'm fighting it. Because I am the one doing the thinking, plain and simple.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses fixed beliefs that another woman is manipulating her husband and stealing from them, maintaining these beliefs despite her husband suggesting she is 'losing her grip'.
